answer.label: Commonly attributed to
answer.sourceLine: The saying is widely credited to Brecht, but no original Brecht work or German text is established here. Wikiquote identifies a longer passage in the newsletter Terra Nossa (1988) as an early located record and explicitly marks the attribution disputed.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Terra Nossa, volumes 1–7 (1988), p. 42, as cited by Wikiquote
The newsletter quotation page was not inspected

source.excerpt: The worst illiterate is the political illiterate.
trail: Wikiquote’s Disputed section ↗ supplies the newsletter lead but notes the absence of a Brecht book citation.
An Eduqas teaching guide ↗ repeats the passage without resolving its source. York’s archive inventory ↗ and WorldCat ↗ are source-finding and metadata evidence only.
source.rightsNote: The exact author, original language and translator are unidentified. The cited newsletter record is modern, and Brecht’s name does not establish a public-domain English text. Only the brief opening sentence is reproduced.

author.name: Bertolt Brecht
author.heading: About Bertolt Brecht
author.bio: Bertolt Brecht developed politically engaged drama and theories of epic theatre that ask spectators to examine social arrangements critically. After years in exile, he settled in East Berlin and founded the Berliner Ensemble with Helene Weigel.

cite.sourceCitation: “The political illiterate,” attributed to Brecht. Newsletter lead: Terra Nossa, vols. 1–7 (1988), 42, as cited by Wikiquote; quotation page uninspected and no Brecht original established.
cite.pageCitation: Quotle.info. “Who really said ‘The worst illiterate is the political illiterate’?” Last verified 9 Nov 2026.

copyAttribution: Commonly attributed to Bertolt Brecht, but unconfirmed; Wikiquote points to an unsourced longer passage in Terra Nossa (1988), not an authenticated Brecht original.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The longer circulating passage ties indifference to politics to the prices of everyday necessities and the conditions of social life. Its appeal explains its use in civic-education settings, including the inspected drama teaching guide.

That political message can resemble Brecht’s concerns without proving his authorship. The newsletter lead is worth following, but its existence and later repetition cannot replace a source in Brecht’s own writing or a documented translation.

schema.faqAnswer: The Brecht attribution is unconfirmed. A newsletter lead and later educational repetition are documented, but no original Brecht text or translator has been established.
